headline: 6 Google Pixel features that are disabled by default but should be enabled
summary: Unlock your Pixel's full potential by enabling these hidden settings for touch sensitivity, notification history, screen attention, adaptive vibration, clear calling, and more.
details: Google Pixel phones offer a clean and user-friendly experience, but many of their most useful features are turned off by default. Enabling these settings can significantly enhance your device's functionality and your daily interaction with it.

If you use a screen protector, Pixel's 'Screen Protector mode' (Settings > Display & touch > Touch sensitivity > Screen Protector mode) increases touch sensitivity to ensure accurate input registration, making typing and gestures feel more responsive.

Never miss an important alert again with 'Notification history' (Settings > Notifications > Notification history). This feature logs recently dismissed notifications, allowing you to review them later, which is invaluable when notifications pile up quickly.

To prevent the screen from dimming while you're reading, 'Screen Attention' (Settings > Display & touch > Screen timeout > Screen attention) uses the front camera to detect if you're looking at the screen, keeping it awake as needed.

'Adaptive Vibration' (Settings > Sound & vibration > Vibration & haptics > Adaptive Vibration) adjusts the phone's vibration intensity based on your environment and usage, making alerts more subtle in quiet settings and more noticeable when you're out and about.

Improve call clarity with 'Clear Calling' (Settings > Sound & vibration > Clear Calling on supported Pixel models). This feature uses on-device processing to reduce background noise, ensuring the person on the other end can hear you better, even in noisy environments.

headline_marked: Slovakia finds [[Russian backdoor]] in traffic cameras, halting deployment
headline: Slovakia finds Russian backdoor in traffic cameras, halting deployment
summary: Security alert issued for NERO R-ONE cameras, which reportedly contain a backdoor granting shell access via SMS from Russian numbers.
details: Slovakia's National Security Service (NBU) has issued a security alert for NERO R-ONE high-speed traffic cameras, halting their planned deployment. The agency claims the cameras contain a backdoor mechanism that allows shell and network access via an SMS message from a list of hardcoded Russian phone numbers.

The NBU's investigation was prompted by accusations that the government purchased cameras from Russia, with media reports linking the deal to a Cyprus shell company with falsified certifications. The cameras are reportedly a rebranded version of the Russian CORDON PRO.M model, produced by St. Petersburg-based firm Semicon.

The cameras were intended for a €30 million EU-funded project to modernize Slovakia's national traffic monitoring system, with 279 units allegedly purchased for deployment on selected roads. The Interior Ministry initially denied Russian origin and claimed the devices would be on a closed network, mitigating data theft risks.

However, an NBU technical report revealed additional security flaws beyond the backdoor. These include a disabled SecureBoot feature, multiple vulnerabilities in the web management portal, and the exposure of live streams without password protection. These findings led the Interior Ministry to pause deployment and order an independent audit.

Similar devices are reportedly in use in Croatia and potentially other Eastern European countries. The NBU's findings raise significant concerns about the security of critical infrastructure when sourced from countries with known security risks.
